details:
**Sleipnir**
Odin's eight-legged horse in Norse myth and the most common giveaway for this answer. The Grimnismal calls it the best of all horses, runes are said to be carved on its teeth, and Hermod rides it down to Hel to try to bring back the dead god Baldr.

**Svadilfari and the building of Asgard's walls**
A giant (a hrimthurs, or frost giant) offered to build Asgard's walls by a deadline, helped only by his powerful stallion Svadilfari. To keep the gods from losing the wager, Loki turned himself into a mare and lured Svadilfari away; the wall went unfinished, and Loki later gave birth to Sleipnir.

**Mares of Diomedes**
Man-eating horses owned by Diomedes, king of the Bistones in Thrace. Capturing them was Heracles' eighth labor; he fed Diomedes to his own horses. Heracles' young companion and lover Abderus was eaten while guarding them, and Heracles founded the city of Abdera near his grave.

**Pegasus**
The winged horse of Greek myth, born from the neck of the beheaded Medusa. Its hoof struck Mount Helicon and opened the Hippocrene spring, which inspired the Muses. Bellerophon tamed it with a golden bridle and rode it against the Chimera, but when he tried to fly up to Olympus, Zeus sent a gadfly that stung Pegasus and threw Bellerophon to the ground.

**Xanthus and Balius**
Achilles' immortal horses, given to his father Peleus by Poseidon as a wedding gift. In Book 19 of the Iliad, Hera gives Xanthus the power of speech, and he warns Achilles that "a great god and powerful Destiny" will cause his death. The Furies (Erinyes) then take away his voice.

**Arion**
An immortal, extremely fast horse born after Poseidon, in the form of a stallion, raped Demeter, who had disguised herself as a mare. In the Arcadian version, the goddess Despoina was born from the same union. Arion carried King Adrastus of Argos to safety, making him the only one of the Seven Against Thebes to survive.

**Gullfaxi**
"Golden Mane," the horse of the giant Hrungnir. Hrungnir bet that Gullfaxi was better than Sleipnir, and Odin staked his head on a race. After Thor killed Hrungnir, he gave Gullfaxi to his young son Magni, who had freed him from under the dead giant's leg.

**Gulltopr**
"Golden Top," the golden-maned horse of Heimdall, the watchman of the Norse gods. Heimdall rides it to Baldr's funeral.

**Epona**
A Celtic and Gallo-Roman goddess of horses and fertility, often shown riding a horse or sitting between horses. Roman cavalry soldiers also worshipped her. The Welsh queen Rhiannon is often thought to be a later version of her.

**Rhiannon**
A heroine of the First Branch of the Welsh Mabinogion who first appears riding a white horse that none of Pwyll's men can catch. After her infant son vanishes, her maids smear a dog's blood on her face so that she is blamed for killing him. As punishment she must sit by the gate, tell visitors her story, and offer to carry them on her back like a horse.

**Arvakr and Alsvidr**
"Early Awake" and "All Swift," the two horses in Norse myth that pull the sun's chariot, driven by Sol. They are always chased across the sky by the wolf Skoll, who will finally swallow the sun at Ragnarok.

**Skinfaxi and Hrimfaxi**
"Shining Mane" and "Frost Mane," the Norse horses ridden by Dagr (Day) and Nott (Night). Skinfaxi's mane lights up the sky and earth, and the foam from Hrimfaxi's bit falls as morning dew.

**"Hector, tamer of horses"**
Hector's most frequent epithet in the Iliad, which also forms the poem's final line, about his funeral. Horses are closely tied to Troy: the city was conquered with the wooden Trojan Horse, and Poseidon, creator of the horse, was its god.

**Horses of Tros and Laomedon**
Zeus gave the Trojan king Tros a set of divine horses to make up for carrying off his son Ganymede. Tros's descendant Laomedon promised these horses to Heracles for saving his daughter Hesione from a sea monster. When Laomedon refused to pay, Heracles sacked Troy.

**Susanoo's flayed horse**
In Japanese Shinto myth, the storm god Susanoo rampages through the weaving hall of his sister, the sun goddess Amaterasu, and throws in a horse he has flayed through a hole in the roof. The horror drives Amaterasu to hide in a cave, which plunges the world into darkness.
